items.title: Show HN: Subvocal – Talk to your computer without making noise
items.body: Hi HN, we're Aarush and Arnav from The Subvocal Company (YC F26) (https://subvocal.company/). We’re building smart glasses that let you talk to your computer without talking out loud. You can mouth words silently and discreetly and the glasses decode them to text at the speed of speech.Here's a video of Dave from YC trying it out: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9QdX1eObVYI(Edit: you don't actually have to move your lips or even open your mouth for this to work! Since the RF can see inside your mouth the system can be fine tuned on "internal speech". This isn't the automatic tongue movements that occur when "thinking" words to yourself, but more like mouthing with your lips closed. It's a bit weird to do, but with practice, we have been able to get it down pretty well.)Arnav and I were studying CS at Georgia Tech at the beginning of the year, with no experience in silent speech or sensing. We were both AI-native builders and power users of Wispr Flow. What bugged us was not being able to use these tools in the library (or an office) or in public. At Stanford’s TreeHacks in February, we decided to build the most technically ridiculous thing we could think of. We’d read about AlterEgo, a silent speech system out of MIT’s Media Lab, and wanted to recreate it in 36 hours. We built a crude prototype, sticking EMG electrodes onto my face:https://drive.google.com/file/d/1mwhv5HZMz3UTevdrgwS5O7g2jWV...We got it to kind of work at a letter level in a very janky way. It wasn’t good enough to win the hackathon, but convinced us to go all in. The first time I typed a sentence without anyone noticing, I felt the magic of the technology.We quickly realized EMG (reading muscle electrical signals) wouldn’t work:- Signal changes due to sweat- Electrical interference- Placement variability- Most importantly, no one wants to stick electrodes onto their face!!So we switched to RF and built the glasses you see now. They emit radio waves, similar to Bluetooth, that pass through your face. As they cross the tongue, lips and soft palate, they’re modulated by silent mouthing. We train foundation models on this data to decode these perturbations to text.Despite prior academic research, getting this to work was a huge engineering challenge. First we built an extremely low noise RF sensing stack. Then we had to place antennas so their fields overlapped maximally with the articulators. Our first attempt on glasses failed completely, so we reverted to old habits and taped antennas on our face:https://drive.google.com/file/d/1ks0dS0eZiTV9EqSFsyB_w5BBjpc...Since taping antennas consistently in the same spot and angle was hard, we created this weird but effective head rig to hold them in place:https://drive.google.com/file/d/1rhzNFpdDzr7oHk0isFY70dkoV4C...This worked, but obviously wasn’t a product yet. So we worked deep in simulations to design glasses that could hold the antennas.That evolved into our design now, with antennas embedded within the frames. Once we established there was a signal, the next hurdle was cross-user generalization. Everyone’s facial anatomy, and hence RF signal patterns, are vastly different. We tried algorithmic workarounds but realized the only lever was to massively scale pretraining data.So that’s what we did. We set up booths in our office and paid people to read prompts wearing our glasses, to pretrain our models on. This produced a beautiful scaling curve, with errors falling quickly as we scaled our dataset and cross-user performance becoming genuinely compelling (as you see in the video above; Dave only had a short 20-sentence calibration).We always heard about building things from first principles but never understood it before this. We tried tackling it top down but completely failed. Only when we broke each component (the antenna, electronics, ML) down to its fundamentals to understand and optimize it did we get it to work really well.Over the next few months we’re continuing R&D to turn our prototype glasses into the slick product on our website and ship in Q1 2027. We’re also scaling up our dataset to improve performance on edge cases.For anyone who loves voice dictation but hates using it around people, we’ve opened preorders for our first batch of 500 units, with a $200 discount off the final price. Allocation is running out quickly, so get yours at https://subvocal.co/preorder!
items.body_ko: 안녕하세요 HN, 저희는 The Subvocal Company (YC F26) (https://subvocal.company/)의 Aarush와 Arnav입니다. 저희는 소리 내어 말하지 않고도 컴퓨터와 대화할 수 있는 스마트 글래스를 개발하고 있습니다. 소리 없이 은밀하게 입 모양으로 단어를 만들면 글래스가 이를 음성 속도로 텍스트로 디코딩합니다.Dave가 YC에서 이 기술을 시도하는 영상입니다: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9QdX1eObVYI(수정: 실제로 입술을 움직이거나 입을 벌리지 않아도 작동합니다! RF가 입안을 볼 수 있으므로 시스템은 "내부 발화(internal speech)"에 대해 미세 조정될 수 있습니다. 이것은 단어를 "생각할" 때 발생하는 무의식적인 혀 움직임이 아니라, 입을 다물고 입 모양을 만드는 것과 더 가깝습니다. 약간 이상하게 느껴지지만, 연습을 통해 저희는 꽤 잘 해낼 수 있었습니다.)Arnav와 저는 올해 초 Georgia Tech에서 CS를 공부하고 있었고, 무음 발화나 센싱 경험은 전혀 없었습니다. 저희 둘 다 AI 네이티브 개발자이자 Wispr Flow의 파워 유저였습니다. 저희를 괴롭혔던 것은 도서관(또는 사무실)이나 공공장소에서 이러한 도구를 사용할 수 없다는 점이었습니다. 2월 Stanford의 TreeHacks에서 저희는 생각할 수 있는 가장 기술적으로 터무니없는 것을 만들기로 결정했습니다. MIT Media Lab의 무음 발화 시스템인 AlterEgo에 대해 읽었고, 36시간 안에 그것을 재현하고 싶었습니다. EMG 전극을 제 얼굴에 붙여서 조잡한 프로토타입을 만들었습니다:https://drive.google.com/file/d/1mwhv5HZMz3UTevdrgwS5O7g2jWV...저희는 매우 엉성한 방식으로 문자 단위로 작동하도록 만들었습니다. 해커톤에서 우승할 만큼 좋지는 않았지만, 저희는 모든 것을 걸기로 결심했습니다. 아무도 눈치채지 못하게 제가 한 문장을 타이핑했던 첫 순간, 저는 이 기술의 마법을 느꼈습니다.저희는 EMG(근육 전기 신호 판독)가 작동하지 않을 것이라는 것을 빠르게 깨달았습니다:- 땀으로 인한 신호 변화- 전기 간섭- 배치 가변성- 가장 중요하게는, 아무도 얼굴에 전극을 붙이고 싶어하지 않습니다!!그래서 저희는 RF로 전환하여 지금 보시는 글래스를 만들었습니다. 이 글래스는 Bluetooth와 유사한 전파를 방출하여 얼굴을 통과합니다. 혀, 입술, 연구개를 통과하면서 무음 입 모양에 의해 변조됩니다. 저희는 이 데이터를 기반으로 파운데이션 모델을 훈련하여 이러한 교란을 텍스트로 디코딩합니다.이전 학술 연구에도 불구하고, 이것을 작동시키는 것은 엄청난 엔지니어링 과제였습니다. 먼저 매우 낮은 노이즈 RF 센싱 스택을 구축했습니다. 그런 다음 안테나를 배치하여 필드가 조음기관과 최대한 겹치도록 해야 했습니다. 글래스에 대한 첫 시도는 완전히 실패했고, 그래서 저희는 옛 습관으로 돌아가 안테나를 얼굴에 테이프로 붙였습니다:https://drive.google.com/file/d/1ks0dS0eZiTV9EqSFsyB_w5BBjpc...안테나를 같은 위치와 각도에 일관되게 테이프로 붙이는 것이 어려웠기 때문에, 저희는 그것들을 제자리에 고정하기 위해 이 이상하지만 효과적인 헤드 리그를 만들었습니다:https://drive.google.com/file/d/1rhzNFpdDzr7oHk0isFY70dkoV4C...이것은 작동했지만, 아직 제품은 아니었습니다. 그래서 저희는 안테나를 장착할 수 있는 글래스를 설계하기 위해 시뮬레이션을 깊이 연구했습니다.그것이 현재 저희의 디자인으로 발전하여, 안테나가 프레임 안에 내장되었습니다. 일단 신호가 있다는 것을 확인한 후, 다음 장애물은 사용자 간 일반화였습니다. 모든 사람의 얼굴 해부학, 따라서 RF 신호 패턴은 매우 다릅니다. 저희는 알고리즘적인 해결책을 시도했지만, 유일한 방법은 사전 훈련 데이터를 대규모로 확장하는 것이라는 것을 깨달았습니다.그래서 저희는 그렇게 했습니다. 저희 사무실에 부스를 설치하고 사람들에게 저희 글래스를 착용하고 프롬프트를 읽도록 돈을 지불하여 모델을 사전 훈련했습니다. 이것은 아름다운 스케일링 곡선을 만들어냈고, 데이터셋을 확장하고 사용자 간 성능이 진정으로 설득력 있게 되면서 오류가 빠르게 감소했습니다(위 영상에서 보시다시피 Dave는 짧은 20문장 보정만 했습니다).저희는 항상 첫 번째 원칙에서부터 무언가를 만드는 것에 대해 들었지만, 이전에는 이해하지 못했습니다. 저희는 상향식으로 접근하려고 시도했지만 완전히 실패했습니다. 각 구성 요소(안테나, 전자 장치, ML)를 기본으로 분해하여 이해하고 최적화했을 때 비로소 정말 잘 작동하게 되었습니다.앞으로 몇 달 동안 저희는 프로토타입 글래스를 웹사이트의 매끄러운 제품으로 만들고 2027년 1분기에 출시하기 위해 R&D를 계속할 것입니다. 또한 엣지 케이스에서의 성능을 향상시키기 위해 데이터셋을 확장하고 있습니다.음성 받아쓰기를 좋아하지만 사람들 앞에서 사용하는 것을 싫어하는 모든 분들을 위해, 저희는 첫 500대 물량에 대해 최종 가격에서 200달러 할인된 가격으로 선주문을 시작했습니다. 물량이 빠르게 소진되고 있으니, 지금 https://subvocal.co/preorder/에서 주문하세요!

items.title: Launch HN: Momentic (YC W24) – Agents that catch bugs by using your app
items.body: Hey HN, we’re Wei-Wei and Jeff. We’re building Momentic, QA agents that autonomously plan, explore, and bug-bash controls and user flows in your web, iOS, Android, and (soon) desktop apps to catch bugs.Here’s a demo: https://youtu.be/BFsM-Se1Fh8We’re both software engineers that spent our careers on dev tooling and infra across companies like Robinhood, Retool, WeWork, and Qualtrics. Testing was always a pain in the ass (esp Playwright and Selenium), so we built agents to do it for us.Modern day software has a ton of bugs and the change failure rate is only growing faster as coding agent adoption scales. LLMs are really good at generating code, but reinforce their own assumptions, write a ton of useless tests, and are bad at visual understanding. On DeepSWE v1.1, Sonnet 5.5 hit 66.2% pass rate when banned from writing tests, versus 65.3% when allowed.OSS end-to-end testing frameworks like Playwright, Selenium, or Maestro force you to hardcode implementation details like XPath, text, or aria-* attributes in your tests. Even with agents, these take a nontrivial amount of time and tokens to build and maintain.In 2023, we saw Nat Friedman drive a browser with GPT-3 via natbot. We were inspired to use this technology to automate the most painful and tedious parts of software engineering: testing. We started with using LLMs to generate and maintain Playwright, but quickly realized that those primitives were fundamentally misaligned with the agentic SDLC. We think the future of QA is agents testing themselves, not writing scripts.Mo is a custom agent harness for catching bugs that builds on the past 3 years of Momentic and millions of test traces from complex, real-world applications. Mo is built for recall: it finds the most real bugs, though Codex is a bit more precise at 86% vs 84%. The tradeoff is cost: Mo costs $2.67 per bug vs $0.80 for Codex, less than Claude Code and Devin.- Self-organizing agent graph. Mo builds a directed acyclic graph (DAG) as it explores. Large product areas automatically fork into parallel sub-agents, each with their own browser or device for concurrent execution.- Specialized agents for domain specific tasks. Planner agents reason over screenshots and video while dedicated locator agents inspect page structure to resolve plain-English interaction targets. Others include image analysis, video understanding, audio generation, and more.- Parallel agents coordinate through cooperative resource leases. Agents can announce that they’re “using” or “modifying” overlapping resources or fixtures. Multiple “using” claims can coexist, but only a single “modifying” claim can be active on any particular one.- Scaled infrastructure. Mo ships with a tunnel that lets users expose private sites and local apps to our hosted agents and infra. A single bug bash can spin up 100s of concurrent browsers and devices.We benchmarked Mo against coding agents on 4 popular open-source apps: Gitea (58.8k stars), Metabase, Twenty (YC), and Saleor, with 1,396 human-labeled bugs. Each agent got the same brief, a fresh E2B sandbox, and no access to source code. Codex and Claude Code used hosted Browserbase browsers, while Devin used its built-in browser. For evaluators, we implemented LLM as a judge (GPT-6.1 Sol) with a human reviewer.Results from a time-boxed 60-minute run:- Mo: 269 bugs, 19.3% recall, 84% precision, $2.67 per bug- Codex (GPT-6.1 Sol + Playwright MCP): 86 bugs, 6.2% recall, 86% precision, $0.80 per bug- Claude Code (Opus 5.5 + Playwright MCP): 59 bugs, 4.2% recall, 80% precision, $4.09 per bug- Devin: 27 bugs, 1.9% recall, 84% precision, $3.89 per bugMo finds more bugs the more time it has. From 30 to 60 minutes, it went from 177 to 269 bugs (+52%), while Codex gained only 16%.Results: https://momentic.ai/qa-benchWrite-up: https://momentic.ai/blog/qa-benchDataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/momentic/qa-benchHarness: https://github.com/momentic-ai/qa-benchWe just shipped PR testing for Vercel and Cloudflare deploy previews and we’re giving every new signup $250 in Mo spend. Paid plans have higher infra capacity and included usage along with options to top up.We’d love for you to try it out and give us feedback. Feel free to comment here, we’ll be around all day!
items.body_ko: 안녕하세요 HN, 저희는 Wei-Wei와 Jeff입니다. 저희는 Momentic을 만들고 있습니다. Momentic은 QA 에이전트로서 웹, iOS, Android, 그리고 (곧) 데스크톱 앱에서 컨트롤과 사용자 흐름을 자율적으로 계획하고, 탐색하고, 버그를 찾아내어 버그를 잡습니다.데모 영상입니다: https://youtu.be/BFsM-Se1Fh8저희 둘 다 Robinhood, Retool, WeWork, Qualtrics와 같은 회사에서 개발 도구 및 인프라 분야에서 경력을 쌓은 소프트웨어 엔지니어입니다. 테스팅은 항상 골칫거리였습니다 (특히 Playwright와 Selenium). 그래서 저희는 이를 대신할 에이전트를 만들었습니다.현대 소프트웨어에는 수많은 버그가 있으며, 코딩 에이전트 도입이 확대됨에 따라 변경 실패율은 점점 더 빨라지고 있습니다. LLM은 코드를 생성하는 데 매우 뛰어나지만, 자체적인 가정을 강화하고, 수많은 쓸모없는 테스트를 작성하며, 시각적 이해에는 능숙하지 않습니다. DeepSWE v1.1에서 Sonnet 5.5는 테스트 작성이 금지되었을 때 66.2%의 통과율을 기록했으며, 허용되었을 때는 65.3%였습니다.Playwright, Selenium, Maestro와 같은 오픈소스 엔드투엔드 테스트 프레임워크는 XPath, 텍스트 또는 aria-* 속성과 같은 구현 세부 정보를 테스트에 하드코딩하도록 강제합니다. 에이전트를 사용하더라도 이를 구축하고 유지하는 데 상당한 시간과 토큰이 소요됩니다.2023년, Nat Friedman이 natbot을 통해 GPT-3로 브라우저를 구동하는 것을 보았습니다. 저희는 이 기술을 사용하여 소프트웨어 엔지니어링에서 가장 고통스럽고 지루한 부분인 테스팅을 자동화하는 데 영감을 받았습니다. 저희는 LLM을 사용하여 Playwright를 생성하고 유지하는 것으로 시작했지만, 이러한 기본 요소들이 에이전트 기반 SDLC와 근본적으로 일치하지 않는다는 것을 빠르게 깨달았습니다. 저희는 QA의 미래는 스크립트를 작성하는 것이 아니라 에이전트가 스스로 테스트하는 것이라고 생각합니다.Mo는 버그를 잡기 위한 맞춤형 에이전트 하네스입니다. 지난 3년간의 Momentic과 복잡한 실제 애플리케이션에서 수백만 건의 테스트 추적을 기반으로 구축되었습니다. Mo는 재현성을 위해 구축되었습니다. 가장 실제적인 버그를 찾아내며, Codex가 86% 대 84%로 약간 더 정확합니다. 트레이드오프는 비용입니다. Mo는 버그당 2.67달러인 반면 Codex는 0.80달러로 Claude Code 및 Devin보다 저렴합니다.- 자체 조직 에이전트 그래프. Mo는 탐색하면서 Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG)를 구축합니다. 대규모 제품 영역은 자동으로 병렬 서브 에이전트로 분기되며, 각 에이전트는 동시 실행을 위해 자체 브라우저 또는 장치를 가집니다.- 도메인별 작업을 위한 전문 에이전트. 플래너 에이전트는 스크린샷과 비디오를 통해 추론하는 반면, 전용 로케이터 에이전트는 페이지 구조를 검사하여 일반 영어 상호작용 대상을 해결합니다. 다른 에이전트에는 이미지 분석, 비디오 이해, 오디오 생성 등이 포함됩니다.- 병렬 에이전트는 협력적 리소스 리스를 통해 조율합니다. 에이전트는 겹치는 리소스 또는 픽스처를 "사용"하거나 "수정"한다고 알릴 수 있습니다. 여러 "사용" 클레임은 공존할 수 있지만, 특정 리소스에 대한 "수정" 클레임은 하나만 활성화될 수 있습니다.- 확장된 인프라. Mo는 사용자가 비공개 사이트와 로컬 앱을 저희 호스팅 에이전트 및 인프라에 노출할 수 있는 터널과 함께 제공됩니다. 단일 버그 스매싱은 수백 개의 동시 브라우저와 장치를 시작할 수 있습니다.저희는 Mo를 Gitea (58.8k stars), Metabase, Twenty (YC), Saleor와 같은 인기 있는 4개의 오픈소스 앱에서 코딩 에이전트와 비교하여 벤치마킹했으며, 1,396개의 사람이 레이블링한 버그가 있었습니다. 각 에이전트는 동일한 브리핑, 새로운 E2B 샌드박스, 그리고 소스 코드 접근 권한 없이 제공되었습니다. Codex와 Claude Code는 호스팅된 Browserbase 브라우저를 사용했으며, Devin은 내장 브라우저를 사용했습니다. 평가를 위해 저희는 인간 검토자가 있는 LLM을 판사 (GPT-6.1 Sol)로 구현했습니다.60분 제한 시간 실행 결과:- Mo: 269개 버그, 19.3% 재현율, 84% 정밀도, 버그당 2.67달러- Codex (GPT-6.1 Sol + Playwright MCP): 86개 버그, 6.2% 재현율, 86% 정밀도, 버그당 0.80달러- Claude Code (Opus 5.5 + Playwright MCP): 59개 버그, 4.2% 재현율, 80% 정밀도, 버그당 4.09달러- Devin: 27개 버그, 1.9% 재현율, 84% 정밀도, 버그당 3.89달러Mo는 시간이 많을수록 더 많은 버그를 찾아냅니다. 30분에서 60분으로 진행하면서 버그가 177개에서 269개로 증가 (+52%)한 반면, Codex는 16%만 증가했습니다.결과: https://momentic.ai/qa-bench작성: https://momentic.ai/blog/qa-bench데이터셋: https://huggingface.co/datasets/momentic/qa-bench하네스: https://github.com/momentic-ai/qa-bench저희는 방금 Vercel과 Cloudflare 배포 미리보기용 PR 테스트를 출시했으며, 모든 신규 가입자에게 Mo 사용료 250달러를 제공하고 있습니다. 유료 플랜은 더 높은 인프라 용량과 포함된 사용량, 그리고 충전 옵션을 제공합니다.저희는 여러분이 Momentic을 사용해보고 피드백을 주시길 바랍니다. 자유롭게 여기에 댓글을 달아주세요. 저희는 하루 종일 여기 있을 것입니다!

items.title: WorkOS reports security breach
items.body: It's not on their website or Trust center yet, but we received the following breach notification from WorkOS:We are writing to notify you of a data security incident that we detected on October 30, 2026 and are continuing to investigate. We value your trust and want to keep you informed while our investigation continues.What HappenedOn October 30, 2026, at 16:39 UTC, WorkOS detected anomalous traffic to an internal business system. Our investigation identified evidence the attack was likely driven by ARTEX, an AI-assisted, autonomous penetration testing framework, from IP addresses based in Hong Kong and China.The unauthorized actor gained access to an internal API used by our sales and marketing tools. Through this service, it was able to access data from our Salesforce and Snowflake instances. These systems hold business contact information, account and commercial information, aggregated and de-identified product usage metrics, marketing contacts, and support tickets. This includes CRM information such as names, email addresses, phone numbers, company mailing addresses, and other business information for WorkOS customers.We have no evidence that your application data was accessed. We also have no evidence that any production WorkOS services were accessed or impacted. Our current analysis indicates this incident was localized to only CRM and customer support data....

items.title: Show HN: Warsaw in voxels – An interactive 3D map of the city centre
items.body:
Explore central Warsaw in voxels - slightly inspired by Minecraft, and MagicaVoxel.
You can change the date, time of day and weather, explore the city, or click on a pedestrian to control them (here a bit of inspiration from Dungeon Keeper).Works best on desktop, but I tried to make it usable on mobile too. The initial load can take a while. It's based on several open datasets, including:- OpenStreetMap (https://www.openstreetmap.org/#map=6/52.02/19.14) - buildings, streets, sidewalks, tram tracks, etc- GUGiK / Geoportal (https://www.geoportal.gov.pl/) - LiDAR for building heights and trees, aerial imagery for colours- Warsaw's city tree database (https://mapa.um.warszawa.pl/) - individual tree species, used for seasonal foliageOpen-source (https://github.com/stared/warsaw-vibe-voxel), so feel invited to (re)use it as you wish!

items.title: Astra can read and write weights to improve Qwen
items.body:
We find that frontier LLMs are surprisingly good at natively reading and writing neural network weights, well past what we’d expect from humans or conventional algorithms. This might be a big deal for both optimization and interpretability.

Just by looking at the raw weights, GPT-6 Astra can tell what a network was trained to do. And without any environment feedback, it has no trouble writing, from scratch, small game-playing networks that outplay networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps.

Likewise, asked to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math without gradients, Astra identifies an issue in its weights causing reasoning loops that Qwen’s own model card warns about, and fixes this by natively editing 0.016% of the weights. With the same sampling settings, this weight correction raises MATH-500 from 7.9% to 48.1% and generalizes out of the box to instruction following, raising IFEval by 3x.

All of this is possible without allowing Astra to write training loops. It uses its reasoning to figure out what each part of a neural network computes, or should compute, and changes the weights accordingly. We call this Weight-Space Programming.

Throughout the history of deep learning, we encoded our simplistic inductive biases into tiny symbolic optimizers like Adam or Muon. This is changing: our neural network weights will soon be natively optimized by LLMs that deliberately reason about their weights.

If you were asked to handcraft a neural network that plays Go, what would you do? If you were handed raw neural network weights and asked to predict their behavior, where would you even start? For almost any human, this is practically impossible.

Today, weights are written by optimization, by custom networks trained to write them, or by compilers from formal programs. In this post, we find that the current generation of frontier LLMs, used natively in natural language, are starting to become eerily good at understanding and crafting neural network weights around natural-language goals.

For a few years now, we’ve all been using LLMs to optimize text artifacts like prompts and the programs built around them . More recently, we’ve started using them to optimize whole harnesses and the training code and hyperparameters that train ML models .

We often justified these methods by reference to the fact that we don’t know other principled ways to hill-climb on text artifacts, unlike for updating the weights of differentiable neural networks. After all, humans can “optimize” code by hand, for example, so it made sense to ask LLMs to do it, but they can’t “optimize” neural weights by hand, so those remained largely in the realm of symbolic algorithms.

In this post, we share very early results that allow us to argue that the paradigm of reasoning-driven optimization is now coming even for differentiable neural networks.

In Weight-Space Programming, a general-purpose LLM reads and writes a network’s weights directly (i.e., not through an optimizer, and in particular not with gradient descent) around some natural language spec, sometimes even with no environment feedback at all.

In natural language, it’s becoming possible to “just ask” an LLM to natively find a hidden trait or failure inside the weights of a neural network, to fix that failure, or to write a new network from scratch. We report early, exciting results on each of these below, first on small networks and then even on real language models:

LLMs can read neural network weights: In Experiments 1 to 3, we ask Astra questions like what game a network was trained to play, what shape is drawn by a diffusion model, and which language a small language model was trained on. In Experiment 7, we ask which of two language models was trained to be sycophantic.

LLMs can fix neural network weights: In Experiment 4, we ask Astra to fix a network that’s failing at some physical control task. In Experiment 8, we ask it to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math, and its fix improves instruction following too.

LLMs can write neural network weights from scratch: In Experiment 5, we ask Astra for networks that play three MinAtar games, and in Experiment 6, for a network that plays Go.

Can LLMs understand model behaviors from weights?

We start with a small-scale experiment to see if LLMs can understand the continuous weight space, which is essentially just a list of numbers.

In our first experiments, we train some neural network with some algorithm. It would be extremely exciting if the LLM is able to tell its behavior just from the weights.

Can Astra tell which game the network was trained on just from the weights?

We trained neural network policies with PPO to play four computer games. All four networks take the same input channels, choose from the same actions, and have exactly the same network dimensions, so that it is not able to tell unless the weights are read.

For each of these networks, we pass its raw weights into Astra as a prompt, and ask: Which game was this neural network trained on? Without revealing the options of the games we consider, Astra was still able to name the right game for all four networks. This is exciting particularly because there are so many games out there that Astra could choose from.

It seems that Astra was able to work out what game each network was built to play, just from features of its weights. For example, where each input channel’s first-layer weights concentrate (e.g., for Breakout, the agent’s weights lie along the bottom row, a paddle), and which actions the output layer tells apart.

Can Astra tell what the diffusion model will generate?

Next, we wanted to see if this generalizes to other tasks and models.

We train diffusion models (DDPM) to generate circle, triangle, and square images independently. We then ask Astra if it could tell what the DDPMs are trained to generate, just from the weights alone. We do not allow tool use or forward passes.

Astra was able to tell what each model generates, from the weights alone. It finds the shape in the output layer, where each hidden unit’s weights draw one piece of the shape’s edge, and it draws just those edges. Interestingly, it draws every shape as an outline, ignoring that the actual models generate filled shapes. This mistake kind of shows it does not rely on calculating the forward pass, but rather it actually reads the structure/geometry of the weights.

Can Astra tell what a language model learned, from the middle of the network alone?

Now, in the first two experiments above, Astra was not really looking at the full network and could get away with only reading the first or the last layers. This is not a scalable strategy for larger (particularly language) models and problems we really care about, as how they process and think through their input often happens in the intermediate layers. So next, we take the first and last layers away and leave Astra with only the middle layers.

We train three small language models (7.2M parameters) to predict the next character, one each on Python codeThe Python code dataset, as a list of its files with a script that rebuilds it: GitHub., Japanese in alphabet (romaji) , and English . We then remove the input and output layers and give Astra only the four transformer blocks in between. Without these two layers, nothing in the weights says which character is which, and the model cannot be run on any text. Astra may analyze the weights with Python, but it may not run the network or any of its layers on any input.

We ask: which language was this network trained on, and what each of its 24 attention heads does. Astra names the right language for all three networks, in both of its attempts. It also finds every copying head (induction head), the heads that let a model repeat text it has seen earlier, and names no other head as one.

The reasoning went like this. To tell Python apart, Astra looked for copying heads, which let a model repeat earlier text, such as completing tot to total when

프론티어 LLM이 신경망 가중치를 원시적으로 읽고 쓰는 데 놀라울 정도로 뛰어나다는 것을 발견했으며, 이는 인간이나 기존 알고리즘이 예상하는 수준을 훨씬 뛰어넘습니다. 이는 최적화와 해석 가능성 모두에 큰 의미를 가질 수 있습니다.

GPT-6 Astra는 원시 가중치만 보고도 네트워크가 무엇을 위해 훈련되었는지 알 수 있습니다. 그리고 어떤 환경 피드백 없이도, PPO로 1억 스텝 동안 훈련된 네트워크를 능가하는 작은 게임 플레이 네트워크를 처음부터 문제없이 작성합니다.

마찬가지로, Astra에게 기울기 없이 Qwen3.5-0.8B의 수학 능력을 향상시키도록 요청하자, Qwen 자체 모델 카드에서 경고하는 추론 루프를 유발하는 가중치의 문제를 식별하고, 가중치의 0.016%를 원시적으로 편집하여 이를 수정합니다. 동일한 샘플링 설정으로 이 가중치 수정은 MATH-500 점수를 7.9%에서 48.1%로 높이고, 바로 instruction following으로 일반화되어 IFEval을 3배 향상시킵니다.

이 모든 것은 Astra에게 훈련 루프를 작성하는 것을 허용하지 않고도 가능합니다. Astra는 추론을 사용하여 신경망의 각 부분이 무엇을 계산하는지, 또는 무엇을 계산해야 하는지 파악하고 그에 따라 가중치를 변경합니다. 우리는 이것을 Weight-Space Programming이라고 부릅니다.

딥러닝 역사 전반에 걸쳐 우리는 Adam이나 Muon과 같은 미세한 상징적 최적화 도구에 단순한 귀납적 편향을 인코딩했습니다. 이것은 변화하고 있습니다. 우리의 신경망 가중치는 곧 가중치에 대해 의도적으로 추론하는 LLM에 의해 원시적으로 최적화될 것입니다.

만약 Go를 플레이하는 신경망을 직접 만들라고 요청받았다면 무엇을 하시겠습니까? 원시 신경망 가중치를 받고 그 동작을 예측하라고 요청받았다면 어디서부터 시작하시겠습니까? 거의 모든 인간에게 이것은 사실상 불가능합니다.

오늘날 가중치는 최적화, 이를 작성하도록 훈련된 사용자 정의 네트워크, 또는 공식 프로그램의 컴파일러에 의해 작성됩니다. 이 게시물에서 우리는 자연어로 원시적으로 사용되는 현재 세대의 프론티어 LLM이 자연어 목표에 맞춰 신경망 가중치를 이해하고 만드는 데 소름 끼치게 능숙해지기 시작한다는 것을 발견합니다.

몇 년 동안 우리는 프롬프트와 그 주변에 구축된 프로그램과 같은 텍스트 아티팩트를 최적화하기 위해 LLM을 사용해 왔습니다. 최근에는 전체 하네스와 ML 모델을 훈련하는 훈련 코드 및 하이퍼파라미터를 최적화하는 데 사용하기 시작했습니다.

우리는 종종 미분 가능한 신경망의 가중치를 업데이트하는 것과는 달리 텍스트 아티팩트에서 언덕 오르기를 할 다른 원칙적인 방법을 알지 못한다는 사실을 언급하며 이러한 방법을 정당화했습니다. 결국, 인간은 코드를 수동으로

items.title: llm 0.37
items.body:
Release: llm 0.37

There's a lot of stuff in this new release of my LLM CLI tool and Python library, representing around two months of accumulated features and fixes.

I added gpt-6.1-sol and gpt-6.1-terra, plus a new llm openai endpoint add command to make it easier to configure additional models that use OpenAI-compatible endpoints.

I switched the default model (if you have not set your own default) to gpt-6-luna - half the price of the previous default, gpt-5.6-luna.

LLM's support for embeddings now accepts that different binary content may have different content-type - necessary for models like Gemini Embedding 2, which can embed text, audio, images, and video.

A lot of open source maintainers complain about a flood of AI-assisted PRs. LLM is my project that has been most affected by this and, to be honest, I'm not finding it to be a problem. That's mainly because I have Opus 5.5 or GPT-6 Astra help me with triage to spot the most useful fixes!

This release includes fixes from 12 authors - almost all AI-assisted - and the burden of reviewing them wasn't nearly as great as I expected. I really see them as bug reports with attached examples - sometimes I land them, sometimes I implement my own fix.

So thanks to 0d00ciallo0721, ac1982, Allen Flux, Bian Yuhan, Bishop Kammeraad, Chen Yufeiyang, Christopher Krah, Ethan Stoner, Jiachen Xie, Olamide Faniyan, Sharat Chandra Sai Boddu, nosmile99 for helping out with (or spending tokens on) this release!

items.title: The U.S. Census Bureau and “Super Intelligence”
items.body:
I was reminded today of AI Adoption Rate Trending Down for Large Companies, a chart produced by Apollo Global Management in September 2025, which appeared to show a slowdown in U.S. corporate AI adoption based on numbers collected by the U.S. Census Bureau. At the time I used that chart to demonstrate GPT-5 data analysis, and then to experiment with Claude's new Code Interpreter. I decided to try running those numbers again to see what had changed over the past year, and in doing so learned that the Bureau has fallen foul of Executive Order 14434, aka the asinine Super Intelligence one.

First, the updated chart

Every two weeks the U.S. Census Bureau runs a survey called the Business Trends and Outlook Survey (aka BTOS). Each time it goes to 200,000 businesses out of 1.2 million total - the surveyed group (a "panel") cycles such that an individual business only completes the survey every twelve weeks.

The latest data is published on alternating Thursdays at 10am.

I used the most recent numbers (published October 22, 2026) to create a new version (GPT-6 Astra Extra High transcript) of the AI adoption chart, updated to reflect both the last twelve months and a change that was made to the survey question sent out by the Bureau:

Here's a link to the larger image.

For comparison, here's that AI adoption chart from last year (my GPT-5 version):

In September 2025 the largest (250+ employees) companies answered "yes" around 12% of the time to the question about whether they used AI in "producing goods or services".

Under the new "any business function" wording, by February 2026, those same large companies answered "yes" around 30% of the time, and by October 2026 that had increased to around 40%.

The data in the above chart comes from the "Employment size class" XLSX file, available from here. Here's a copy of the file I used.

You can view the survey document that is sent out to businesses - here's my snapshot copy of that 346KB PDF.

The changing language of the questions

As the chart demonstrates, the question asked by the Bureau changed in a material way on November 17th, 2025. Prior to that date, the question they asked was this (emphasis mine):

In the last two weeks, did this business use Artificial Intelligence (AI) in producing goods or services? (Examples of AI: machine learning, natural language processing, virtual agents, voice recognition, etc.)

On December 3rd, 2025, the Bureau announced a significant change to that question. Here's the replacement:

In the last two weeks, did this business use Artificial Intelligence (AI) in any of its business functions? (Examples of AI: machine learning, natural language processing, virtual agents, voice recognition, etc.)

No more "producing goods or services" - now it's "in any of its business functions"! This means that the answers to the question before and after November 17th are not directly comparable.

From October 19, 2026, they ask about Super Intelligence

When I went looking for the updated question language in the latest XLSX file, I couldn't find it. I found this instead:

In the last two weeks, did this business use Super Intelligence or SI (formerly referred to as Artificial Intelligence or AI) in any of its business functions? (Examples of SI use include: SI-powered data analysis; generative SI for marketing, product design, or coding; virtual SI agents for customer service; SI-powered forecasting or pricing; SI-driven computer vision for quality control, etc.)

The BTOS about page explains what happened:

Beginning with the October 19, 2026 collection, instrument wording was updated due to Executive Order 14434.

The current numbers reflect the old Artificial Intelligence survey wording - the first survey results reflecting the Super Intelligence wording are due for publication on Thursday.

Is this going to affect the survey?

The obvious open question here is whether this wording change is going to affect the survey results.

The businesses answering this survey will have last seen that question twelve weeks ago, when it was still called AI. Hopefully the new language isn't going to confuse them, especially since the survey helpfully spells out "formerly referred to as Artificial Intelligence or AI".

I can't help but laugh at the absurdity of "SI-powered data analysis; generative SI for marketing, product design, or coding; virtual SI agents for customer service" though.

items.title: If in doubt, delete the uv.lock file
items.body:
I've been getting the occasional confusing Python dependency error since switching over to Python 3.15 and the rule I'm having to remember is:

If in doubt, delete the uv.lock file

Most of my projects are libraries which don't include a uv.lock file, since it's rude for a library dependency to lock versions for anything else that uses it.

Running uv run pytest etc tends to leave uv.lock files lying around, which are listed in .gitignore and so do not get committed to my repositories.

But... sometimes that uv.lock pins a version of a dependency that doesn't yet have a Python 3.15 wheel. An example from earlier today:

error: Failed to build `watchfiles==1.1.1`
cause: Call to `maturin.build_wheel` failed

error: the configured Python interpreter version (3.15) is newer
than PyO3's maximum supported version (3.14)

Deleting that file and running uv run pytest again usually fixes the problem.

items.title: Building AI for Lawyers - Jacob Lauritzen, CTO of Legora
items.body:
In this episode, we chat with Jacob Lauritzen, CTO of Legora, following the announcement of their $550M Series E at an $8.8B valuation a couple weeks ago. We talk about what it takes to build AI agents for lawyers and what other people building agents can learn from that work.

Legora started in a Stockholm basement with a simple product: ChatGPT, Swedish law, and a search tool. Jacob had already been through YC with his own startup when he helped Max Junestrand with the application for Leya (now Legora). He later joined as head of engineering and is now CTO.

Today the agent drafts and edits Word documents, reviews thousands of contracts at once, and coordinates work between lawyers, their clients, and other agents. The company passed $100 million in ARR in April, less than 18 months after launch, and now has more than 1,800 customers. It raised $550 million in March at a $5.55 billion valuation, then another $550 million in October at an $8.8 billion valuation. Its latest acquisition, Wexler, was its fifth just this year.

We asked Jacob how you evaluate agents when you can't see your customers' data, which tasks still need better models, how legal engineers and forward deployed engineers split the work, and why the billable hour as a business model is being upended.

Watch the full conversation on YouTube →

Open video on YouTube ↗

What changed for the billable hour?

When Jacob first read Leya's YC application, he had one piece of feedback: people had tried building legal tech a million times, and it never worked. If lawyers bill by the hour, getting faster means earning less. Why would they buy a tool that does that?

What changed, he says, is the pressure on firms. In the US, routine work like small reviews is already shifting to flat project fees. Some firms do it for free to hold on to the client. The money moves to M&A, litigation, and time spent with clients.

We asked whether that means firms will stop needing paralegals and junior lawyers. Jacob says that's not what Legora is seeing. A good junior is worth more today than two years ago because they get so much more done, just as in engineering.

Jump to the billing model discussion →

Evals without access to customer data

Most teams improve their agents by reading traces. Legora can't read any. Almost everything users upload is confidential, and much of it belongs to the firm's clients, not the firm.

So the evals team has to recreate the kinds of work customers do. Three engineers and three lawyers build RL environments to simulate the work their customers do. One example is a 10,000-file data room where the agent runs due diligence and has to produce a report that catches the right red flags. The team plots the results on a heat map by practice area and task. A new model often gets better at some kinds of legal work and worse at others.

The team draws on a pool of about 100 legal engineers: lawyers who spent three or four years in big law, often with a CS degree. In production, Legora classifies failures into 10 to 20 known failure modes and runs cheap LLM-based checks behind feature flags.

Those restrictions also determine which infrastructure Legora can use. Everything runs on Azure because when Legora started, law firms wouldn't accept AWS or GCP, and Microsoft was already an approved vendor through 365.

Jump to evals without traces →

Where smarter models still matter

Legora resisted a model picker for a long time before giving in. Jacob's view is that a lawyer shouldn't have to decide whether a contract is a Sonnet-high or an Opus-mid task. It's Legora's job to find the best available tradeoff between quality, cost, latency, governance, and regional availability.

He estimates that models already handle about 60% of legal work really well. For those tasks it's a cost and latency problem now. Complex analysis and editing across million-token contracts still need more intelligence.

Legora has started post-training open-weight models for narrow tasks like legal research, with no plans to train its own frontier model. For drafting, Jacob finds Fable and Opus too verbose. Astra is more concise. To address hallucinations, everything the agent writes gets a citation that highlights a bounding box in the source PDF, multiple layers down.

Jump to the model discussion →

A few building blocks, many products

Six months into the job, Jacob showed the team a slide of the 300 Spartans and declared that Legora would stay at 20 engineers forever. It now has 100, and he says that still feels too small. His job now is to build a system where the team can ship just a few things and customers feel like they're getting a lot.

The team builds around a few primitives: projects that hold files, the agent, Tabular Review, and lists. Lists are a flexible Notion-style database with triggers and automations. Agents can create and read lists, and changes to a list can start an agent. Intake is a Slack bot that turns a request into a ticket on a list.

Tabular Review is the one the industry copied, down to the name. Each row is a document, each column is a question. Drop in 10,000 employment contracts and ask for the termination period, the IP assignment clause, and the severance terms. It supports up to a million cells, but starts with just 10 rows so you can fix your prompts before running the rest.

Legal engineers configure new products on these primitives without writing code. Even Wexler's fact intelligence product runs on the same building blocks.

Jump to the primitives discussion →

Legal engineers first, forward deployed engineers second

Legora hired its first forward deployed engineer about nine months ago in New York: Di Qi, a two-time YC founder who worked on search at Meta. Legal engineers configure the product the way a power user would and don't write code. Forward deployed engineers write code into production, build integrations into a firm's CRM or document management system, and push what they learn back into the core product. They still don't touch client data.

When a big, engaged client signs, Legora assigns legal engineers to work with them and adds an FDE if the project needs one. Within a year, Jacob expects to have a rotating group of FDEs who sit with a client for a couple of months, build what they need, and move on.

Jump to the forward deployed discussion →

Where this goes

In two years, Jacob thinks big enterprises will use Legora through tools like Claude Cowork, while law firms work inside Legora directly. He doesn't expect the labs to cut Legora off the way they've done to coding companies. For a $400 million M&A deal, he thinks people will still want Legora.

Jump to the predictions →

items.title: Building Legal Agents When You Can't See the Data - Jacob Lauritzen, CTO of Legora
items.body:
Legora can’t read a single trace of what its agent does for a lawyer. The data belongs to the law firm’s clients. How do you build and test an agent when you can’t see its work?
Jacob Lauritzen is the CTO of Legora, one of the fastest-growing companies in legal tech history. The team started in a Stockholm basement with ChatGPT, Swedish law, and a search tool. Today, a lawyer can use Legora to draft and edit Word documents, review 10,000 contracts in a single table, or run due diligence. The agent also coordinates work between lawyers, clients, and other agents. When Legora made its own acquisitions, the team used it for diligence.
What we talked about
• Why Legora resisted adding a model picker for years, and why it finally added one
• Jacob’s estimate that models already do about 60% of legal work well, and why the rest takes a smarter model
• How three engineers and three lawyers build test environments modeled on customers’ work, much like the “worlds” used in reinforcement learning
• A citation problem where the model got it right 70% of the time, then 99% after one release. Legora didn’t have to change anything.
• Why Legora runs everything on Azure and why it doesn’t use ElevenLabs
• Tabular Review, the million-cell spreadsheet the industry copied down to the name
• How intake works, how agents create lists, and how a list can start another agent
• What legal engineers and forward-deployed engineers each do, and who gets to write code
• The 300 Spartans slide Jacob used to argue that 20 engineers would be enough forever. Now there are 100, and he still feels short-handed.
• Why Jacob finds Fable and Opus too chatty for drafting and likes Astra’s concise writing
• Why drafting a long contract is a search problem
• Whether model labs will cut off legal tools the way they cut off coding tools
• What happens to law firm partnerships, the billable hour, and jobs for junior lawyers
Legora is hiring engineers in New York, Stockholm, and London.

items.body_ko:
Legora는 에이전트가 변호사를 위해 수행하는 작업의 흔적을 전혀 읽을 수 없습니다. 데이터는 로펌 고객의 것입니다. 에이전트의 작업을 볼 수 없을 때 어떻게 에이전트를 구축하고 테스트할 수 있을까요?
Jacob Lauritzen은 법률 기술 역사상 가장 빠르게 성장하는 회사 중 하나인 Legora의 CTO입니다. 이 팀은 스톡홀름의 지하에서 ChatGPT, 스웨덴 법률, 그리고 검색 도구로 시작했습니다. 오늘날 변호사는 Legora를 사용하여 Word 문서를 작성하고 편집하거나, 단일 테이블에서 10,000개의 계약을 검토하거나, 실사를 수행할 수 있습니다. 에이전트는 또한 변호사, 고객 및 다른 에이전트 간의 업무를 조정합니다. Legora가 자체적으로 인수를 했을 때, 팀은 이를 실사에도 사용했습니다.
우리가 이야기 나눈 내용
• Legora가 수년 동안 모델 피커 추가를 거부한 이유와 마침내 추가하게 된 이유
• Jacob은 모델이 이미 법률 업무의 약 60%를 잘 수행하고 있으며, 나머지는 더 똑똑한 모델이 필요하다고 추정합니다.
• 세 명의 엔지니어와 세 명의 변호사가 강화 학습에 사용되는 “세계”와 유사하게 고객의 작업을 모델로 삼아 테스트 환경을 구축하는 방법
• 모델이 처음에는 70% 정확했지만, 한 번의 릴리스 후 99%로 올라간 인용 문제. Legora는 아무것도 변경할 필요가 없었습니다.
• Legora가 모든 것을 Azure에서 실행하고 ElevenLabs를 사용하지 않는 이유
• 산업계가 이름까지 복사한 백만 셀 스프레드시트, Tabular Review
• 인테이크가 작동하는 방식, 에이전트가 목록을 생성하는 방식, 그리고 목록이 다른 에이전트를 시작할 수 있는 방식
• 법률 엔지니어와 전개 엔지니어(forward-deployed engineers)가 각각 무엇을 하며, 누가 코드를 작성하는지
• Jacob이 20명의 엔지니어로 충분하다고 주장하는 데 사용했던 300명의 스파르탄 슬라이드. 이제는 100명인데도 여전히 인력이 부족하다고 느낍니다.
• Jacob이 Fable과 Opus는 초안 작성에 너무 말이 많고, Astra의 간결한 작성을 좋아하는 이유
• 긴 계약서를 작성하는 것이 검색 문제인 이유
• 모델 랩이 코딩 도구를 차단한 것처럼 법률 도구를 차단할 것인가
• 로펌 파트너십, 시간당 청구 방식, 주니어 변호사 일자리에 어떤 일이 일어날 것인가
Legora는 뉴욕, 스톡홀름, 런던에서 엔지니어를 고용하고 있습니다.
